d: Software that takes a goal, decides its own steps, and uses tools to get there - instead of following a fixed script. It loops: think, act, check the result, try again.
w: This is the shift everyone's talking about. A chatbot answers you; an agent goes and does the thing.

d: A process where an AI model runs several steps on its own, with checkpoints where a human or another system can step in.
w: Most real business automation lands here - not full autonomy, not a single prompt.

d: The work of making a model behave the way people actually intend, including when nobody wrote a rule for the situation.
w: It's why two models with similar raw ability can feel very different to work with.

d: A way for your code to talk to a service. You send a request, you get a structured response back.
w: Anything beyond copy-pasting into a chat window goes through an API.

d: A private string that identifies your account when you call an API. Treat it like a password.
w: Leaked keys get scraped from public repos within minutes and run up real bills.

d: A hypothetical system that can handle any intellectual task a person can, rather than being good at a narrow set.
w: Nothing shipping today is AGI. When a vendor implies otherwise, that's marketing.

d: The broad field of getting machines to do things we'd call intelligent - recognising, predicting, reasoning, generating.
w: It's an umbrella, not a product. Ask what's underneath when someone says a tool is "AI-powered".

d: The mechanism that lets a model weigh which earlier words matter most when producing the next one.
w: It's the idea that made transformers work, and the reason models track context across long passages.

d: A fixed set of tasks used to score models against each other. MMLU, SWE-bench, GPQA and friends.
w: Useful for rough ranking. A benchmark win rarely predicts whether a model is good at your job.

d: Skew in a model's output that traces back to skew in its training data or design choices.
w: It shows up quietly - in who gets shortlisted, whose accent transcribes badly, which photo it picks.

d: Getting a model to write out its intermediate reasoning before answering, rather than jumping to a conclusion.
w: Cheapest accuracy upgrade there is on multi-step problems. Just ask it to work through the steps.

d: Cutting documents into smaller passages before storing them for retrieval.
w: Bad chunking is the number one reason a RAG system returns nonsense. Split on meaning, not character count.

d: A coding agent that works in your terminal or editor - it reads your repo, edits files, runs commands, and opens pull requests.
w: Different from autocomplete. You hand it a task, not a line.

d: The maximum amount of text a model can hold in view at once - your prompt, the conversation so far, and its reply, all counted in tokens.
w: Run past it and the earliest content silently drops. It's usually the reason a long chat "forgets".

d: Machine learning using neural networks with many layers, trained on large datasets.
w: Every model you've heard of in the last decade sits in this category.

d: Training a small model to copy the behaviour of a big one.
w: How you get near-frontier quality at a fraction of the cost and latency.

d: A list of numbers representing a piece of text, image or audio, arranged so similar things sit close together.
w: The trick behind semantic search - it finds meaning, not keyword matches.

d: Your own test set for checking whether a prompt, model or agent does the job on your data.
w: Without evals you're guessing. This is what separates a demo from something you can ship.

d: How well you can tell why a model produced a particular output.
w: Regulated industries will ask. "The model said so" isn't an answer in a lending or hiring decision.

d: Including a handful of worked examples in your prompt so the model matches the pattern.
w: Faster and cheaper than fine-tuning, and it fixes most format problems on its own.

d: Further training a pre-trained model on your own examples so it picks up a specific style, format or domain.
w: Reach for it when prompting plateaus - and after you've tried retrieval first.

d: A large model trained on broad data that gets adapted to many downstream tasks.
w: You rent these rather than build them. Training one costs more than most companies are worth.

d: Letting a model return a structured request to run one of your functions, with arguments filled in.
w: The bridge between text generation and doing something real - booking, querying, sending.

d: Models that produce new content - text, images, code, audio - instead of only classifying or predicting.
w: The part of AI that got everyone's attention in 2022 and hasn't let go.

d: Tying a model's answer to specific source material it was given, so claims trace back to something real.
w: An ungrounded answer sounds identical to a grounded one. That's the whole problem.

d: Checks around a model that block bad inputs or outputs - policy filters, schema validation, spend limits.
w: Agents especially need them. Anything that can act can act wrongly.

d: When a model states something false with complete confidence - an invented citation, a plausible wrong number.
w: It's not a bug they'll patch out. Design your process to verify anything that matters.

d: A checkpoint where a person reviews or approves before the automation continues.
w: The difference between an agent that drafts the email and one that sends it to 4,000 customers.

d: Running a trained model to get an answer. The everyday act of using AI.
w: Training is a one-off cost. Inference is the bill that arrives every month.

d: A prompt crafted to get a model to ignore its own rules.
w: Assume anything user-facing will be probed. Filter what comes out, not just what goes in.

d: The date after which a model has no built-in knowledge of world events.
w: Ask about last week and you'll get confident nonsense unless the model can search.

d: A model trained on enormous amounts of text to predict what comes next, which turns out to be enough to write, summarise, translate and reason.
w: GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Qwen - all LLMs. Everything else is packaging around them.

d: How long a model takes to respond - often measured as time to the first token, then tokens per second.
w: A model that's 5% smarter but three times slower loses in most real products.

d: A cheap fine-tuning method that trains a small set of extra weights instead of the whole model.
w: Puts custom models within reach of a laptop budget rather than a data centre one.

d: Getting a system to learn patterns from data instead of being programmed with explicit rules.
w: The engine under almost everything labelled AI, including the boring, useful stuff.

d: An open standard for connecting models to tools and data sources, so one integration works across different apps and models.
w: Stops every AI tool needing its own bespoke plug for your Gmail, Notion or database.

d: A model that handles more than one kind of input or output - text plus images, audio or video.
w: Screenshots, whiteboards, PDFs and invoices become usable input.

d: An open-source workflow tool where you wire together triggers, apps and AI steps visually, then self-host it.
w: The fastest route from 'we should automate this' to something running, without writing a backend.

d: Layers of simple maths units with adjustable weights, tuned by training until the whole thing maps inputs to useful outputs.
w: You don't need the maths to use one - but knowing it's statistics, not magic, sets your expectations right.

d: A model whose trained weights you can download and run yourself. Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek.
w: You control the data, the cost and the uptime. You also own the ops.

d: Coordinating several models, tools and steps into one reliable process, with retries and error handling.
w: Where most agent projects actually succeed or fail. The model is the easy part.

d: The learned numbers inside a model. '70B' means 70 billion of them.
w: More parameters usually means more capable and more expensive - but training quality matters more than raw size.

d: The first, giant training run where a model learns general patterns from a broad dataset.
w: Months of compute and a nine-figure bill. Everything after this is comparatively cheap.

d: Everything you send the model - instructions, context, examples, the actual question.
w: The single biggest lever on output quality, and the only one that's free.

d: Reusing the processed form of a repeated chunk of prompt instead of paying to process it again.
w: Long system prompts and big documents get much cheaper and faster on repeat calls.

d: Writing and refining prompts systematically - clear instructions, examples, structure, constraints - until output is reliable.
w: Less mystical than it sounds. It's mostly being specific and testing.

d: Hiding instructions inside content a model will read - a webpage, an email, a PDF - to hijack what it does next.
w: The top security risk for agents. If your agent reads untrusted text, assume it can be talked into things.

d: Storing a model's numbers at lower precision so it needs less memory and runs faster.
w: How a 70B model ends up running on a decent laptop with only a small quality hit.

d: Fetching relevant documents at question time and handing them to the model so it answers from your material.
w: The standard way to make a general model useful on private, current company data.

d: A cap on how many requests or tokens you can send in a window.
w: Hits hardest at demo time. Build in retries with backoff before you need them.

d: A model trained to spend extra compute working through a problem internally before answering.
w: Worth the extra seconds and cost on hard problems. Overkill for summarising an email.

d: Training a model on human preferences between candidate answers, so it learns which responses people actually want.
w: The step that turned raw text predictors into assistants worth talking to.

d: Searching by meaning rather than exact words, using embeddings.
w: Finds the doc about 'staff leave policy' when someone searched 'time off'.

d: Sending the response token by token as it's generated instead of waiting for the whole thing.
w: Same total time, far better experience. Users watch progress rather than a spinner.

d: Forcing a model to reply in a fixed shape - valid JSON matching a schema you define.
w: Turns text into something your code can use without brittle parsing.

d: Standing instructions that sit above the conversation - role, tone, rules, what to refuse.
w: Where you encode your product's behaviour. Users see the results, never the text.

d: A setting for randomness. Low temperature gives consistent, predictable text; high gives varied, surprising text.
w: Near zero for extraction and classification. Higher for brainstorming and copy.

d: The chunks a model reads and writes - roughly three-quarters of a word each in English.
w: You're billed per token and limited by tokens. It's the unit of everything.

d: Giving a model access to real capabilities - search, a database query, a calculator, an API call - that it can invoke when needed.
w: Turns a model that talks about your data into one that reads it.

d: The material a model learns from.
w: Its blind spots, biases and cutoff date all trace back here.

d: The neural network architecture, introduced in 2017, behind nearly every modern language model.
w: The 'T' in GPT. It's why progress accelerated so sharply.

d: A database built to store embeddings and find the nearest matches fast.
w: The memory layer for retrieval. Start with pgvector before buying anything.

d: Building software by describing what you want to a coding agent and steering the result, rather than writing most lines yourself.
w: Great for prototypes. Still needs review before anything touches production.

d: Asking a model to do a task with no examples, just instructions.
w: Try this first. Modern models handle far more zero-shot than people expect.
